title: The urinary system, fluids, and acid-base balance
note: Each nephron filters plasma at the glomerulus, then reabsorbs most of the filtrate and secretes some wastes along the tubule. About 180 L is filtered daily but only 1 to 2 L becomes urine. ADH adds water channels to collecting ducts, and aldosterone boosts Na+ recovery. Buffers, the lungs, and the kidneys hold blood pH near 7.4.

read.title: 180 liters a day
text: The kidneys filter the entire plasma volume dozens of times a day. In each nephron, blood enters the glomerulus through an afferent arteriole and leaves through a narrower efferent arteriole, which keeps glomerular pressure high. About 55 mm Hg of blood pressure pushes fluid out, opposed by about 15 mm Hg of pressure in the capsule and 30 mm Hg of colloid osmotic pressure from plasma proteins. The net 10 mm Hg forces water and small solutes through the fenestrated capillary wall, basement membrane, and podocyte slits, while blood cells and most proteins stay behind.

That produces about 180 liters of filtrate a day, yet only 1 to 2 liters leave as urine. The tubule recovers the rest. The proximal convoluted tubule reclaims about two-thirds of the water and sodium and nearly all of the glucose and amino acids. The loop of Henle builds a salty gradient in the medulla: its descending limb lets water out, and its thick ascending limb pumps salt out but holds water in.

The final adjustment happens in the distal tubule and collecting duct, under hormonal control. Aldosterone increases sodium recovery, and ADH inserts aquaporins so water can leave the collecting duct into the salty medulla. With plenty of ADH, urine is small in volume and concentrated; with little ADH, it is large and dilute.
